public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 943

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/943](https://www.erdosproblems.com/943)
-/

@[expose] public section

open AdditiveCombinatorics Nat Filter

namespace Erdos943

/--
Let $A$ be the set of powerful numbers. Is is true that $1_A\ast 1_A(n)=n^{o(1)}$ for every $n$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_943 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ (o : ℕ → ℝ), o =o[atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ) ∧ ∀ᶠ n in atTop, (sumRep Powerful n) ≤ (n : ℝ)^(o n) := by
  sorry

end Erdos943

reformulations.difference: The source asks whether $1_A\ast 1_A(n)=n^{o(1)}$ 'for every n'. The Lean states an upper bound with an explicit witness: ∃ o : ℕ → ℝ, o =o[atTop] 1 ∧ ∀ᶠ n in atTop, (sumRep Powerful n : ℝ) ≤ (n:ℝ)^(o n). It uses '≤' where the source writes '=', and 'for all sufficiently large n' where the source writes 'for every n'.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Reading '=' as '≤': for a counting function, 'r(n) = n^{o(1)}' conventionally means r(n) ≤ n^{o(1)}, i.e. r(n) ≪_ε n^ε. A literal two-sided equality is impossible whenever r(n) = 0, and #eval shows 414 of the integers in [1000, 2000) have no representation as a sum of two positive powerful numbers. The ulam.ai write-up (Chojecki, 2026) reads the question the same way and proves the partial bound r(n) ≪ n^{2/5+ε}. Equivalence of forms, proved in Lean for every r : ℕ → ℕ: (∃ o, o =o[atTop] 1 ∧ ∀ᶠ n, r n ≤ n^(o n)) ↔ ∀ ε : ℝ, ε > 0 → ∀ᶠ n, r n ≤ n^ε. The witness for ← is o(n) = log(max(r n,1))/log n; → uses rpow monotonicity in the exponent for base ≥ 1. 'Eventually' vs 'every n': an o(1) exponent is an asymptotic notion, and finitely many n ≥ 2 can be absorbed by changing o at finitely many points. A literal ∀ n would also fail spuriously at n ≤ 1 because of Lean's conventions (1^x = 1, while sumRep Powerful 1 = 2). The past fix to Erdős 942 (PR #1526) made exactly this ∀ → ∀ᶠ change.

reformulations.difference: Nat.Powerful (= Nat.Full 2) holds for 0 (primeFactors 0 = ∅). So sumRep Powerful n also counts the pairs (0, n) and (n, 0) when n is powerful. Checked by #eval for n < 3000: sumRep Powerful n = r(n) + 2·[n powerful] for n ≥ 1, where r(n) counts ordered pairs of positive powerful numbers, the source's A.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Pointwise r(n) ≤ sumRep Powerful n ≤ r(n) + 2 (proved in Lean via a Finset subset argument). Adding at most 2 does not affect 'for every ε > 0, eventually ≤ n^ε': once n^{ε/2} ≥ 2 we have n^{ε/2} + 2 ≤ n^ε. Proved in Lean: the file's right-hand side, copied verbatim and checked by rfl to be the theorem's type, is equivalent to ∀ ε : ℝ, ε > 0 → ∀ᶠ n in atTop, rPos n ≤ n^ε, with rPos n = #{(a,b) : a+b=n, a,b ≥ 1 powerful}. #print axioms shows only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. On positive integers Nat.Powerful agrees with the source's 'p | n ⇒ p² | n': proved in Lean, and brute-force checked for n < 2000. Ordered vs unordered pairs (OEIS A085252 counts unordered) differ by at most a factor 2, which is also immaterial.

review.notes: No findings. Checked on its own terms, the single declaration Erdos943.erdos_943 is a faithful formalization of erdosproblems.com/943. The Lean proof that its right-hand side is equivalent to 'for every ε > 0, r(n) ≤ n^ε for large n' (r = ordered pairs of positive powerful numbers) is in /workspace/review/equiv.lean. The check that the copied statement is literally the theorem's type is in /workspace/review/check_same.lean. The category `research open` matches the source ('OPEN — cannot be resolved with a finite computation'; teorth/erdosproblems data: open). The ulam.ai note (March 2026) gives only partial results. answer(sorry) is Prop-typed and the right-hand side is the positive form of the question, so this is not a negated conjecture. The original Er76d paper (users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1976-39.pdf) is a scanned PDF with no text layer and no OCR tool was available, so the wording was checked against erdosproblems.com, the source the file cites. Cosmetic only, not reported: the theorem docstring has a typo ('Is is true') and omits the source's parenthetical definition of powerful numbers.
